The Schmitt critic Gerhard Leibholz (1901–1982) became a judge on the Federal Constitutional Court in 1951 and later one of the most influential judges in the Court’s history.

“poor Kriesenhahn” — Schmitt means Ernst Friesenhahn, who in the 1950 Festschrift for Richard Thoma had, in Ernst Forsthoff’s words, “perfidiously disowned” his teacher, and who criticized Schmitt when he took office as rector in Bonn in November 1950. See van Laak, pp. 154–55; BW Huber, pp. 331 and 377.
quod licet Jovi, non licet bovi — “What Jupiter is allowed to do, the ox is certainly not allowed to do.” Roman saying.
“Miorița fate” — See above, note to p. 201.
In his essay “Die Einheit der Welt,” Schmitt writes:

“For in the end it would be a sorry state of affairs if the dualism of the present world amounted to nothing more than the contrast between birth control and animus procreandi, so that every newborn child entered the world as an aggressor and was immediately drawn into the modern system of criminalization.”
C. Schmitt, “Die Einheit der Welt.” In: Merkur 6, 1952, p. 8. Reprinted in SGN, pp. 496–512.

“Hans Peters, director of studies at the Nazi Academy of Administration …” — Although Peters was a member of the Kreisau Circle, before 1945 he published writings that conformed to the National Socialist regime. Schmitt wrote to Forsthoff about him on 3 September 1949:
“What you write about Hans Peters agrees with the experiences I have had with him since 1945: intellectually as well as morally, a specimen of the ruling third-rate set.”
BW Forsthoff, p. 53; see also BW Huber and above, note to p. 204.
“Serge Maiwald died on 22 February …” — This note was expanded into the obituary; see above, note to p. 212.
Miching mallecho — Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 2. Hamlet to Ophelia:
“Marry, this is miching mallecho; it means mischief.”
See Schmitt’s reference in Hamlet oder Hekuba, Stuttgart 1985, p. 68, note 1, to Laura Bohannan, “Miching Mallecho. That Means Witchcraft.” In: The London Magazine 1, 1954, no. 5, pp. 51–60.
“Power is evil in itself” and “God is dead” —
“And now power is evil in itself.”
Jacob Burckhardt, Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen, Kröners Taschenausgabe 55, Stuttgart 1978, p. 97.
Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science, section 125.
“You, Earth, remained steadfast through this night as well” — Schmitt ended his 1955 radio “Conversation on the New Space,” broadcast by Hessischer Rundfunk, as follows:

“You surely know how the second part of Goethe’s Faust begins. Faust awakens after a night filled with terrible dreams and feels the happiness of a new earthly morning, which gives him comfort and strength, the happiness of a new beginning. And so he greets the new world now opening before him with the magnificent line:
You, Earth, remained steadfast through this night as well.

“In the same way, I believe that after a terrible night threatened by atomic bombs and similar horrors, mankind will one morning awaken and gratefully recognize itself once again as the child of the firmly grounded Earth.”
C. Schmitt, Gespräch über die Macht und den Zugang zum Machthaber. Gespräch über den neuen Raum, Berlin 1994, p. 64.

“Conclusion of my Duisburg lecture” — As part of the Lower Rhine University Weeks, Schmitt gave a lecture in Duisburg on 21 April 1952 entitled “Die Einheit der Welt.” It was largely identical to the essay of the same name published in Merkur, no. 47, 1952, pp. 1–11. It ends:

“But just as the Earth remains greater than the dilemma posed by this dualistic question, so history remains stronger than every philosophy of history. For that reason, I do not regard the present division of the world into two as a preliminary stage on the way to unity, but as a passage toward a new plurality.”
See also G. Maschke’s note to the republication in SGN, pp. 510–12.
“Wonderful passage in Buffon” — Georges-Louis Leclerc de Buffon, Histoire naturelle, générale et particulière, avec la description du Cabinet du Roy, vols. 1–15, Paris 1749–1767.
The quotation in Rousseau reads, in Heinrich Meier’s German edition:
“Since plants draw far more of the substance they need for nourishment from air and water than from the earth, it follows that when they decay, they return more to the earth than they took from it …”
J. J. Rousseau, Diskurs über die Ungleichheit, ed. H. Meier, Paderborn 1984, p. 285.
renegatur et rejiciatur Norma — “The norm is denied and rejected.”
In his encyclical Summi Pontificatus of 20 October 1939, Pope Pius XII lamented the “denial and rejection of the norms of natural law,” which he identified as one of the causes of the war.
“Norma, Norma, you have vanished” — An allusion to Friedrich von Flotow’s opera Martha, oder der Markt zu Richmond. In Act 3, Scene 4, the aria “Ach! so fromm, Ach! So traut” contains the line:

“Interjections by H. Heller and A. Arndt” — Hermann Heller, counsel for Prussia in the Prussia v. Reich case before the State Court in Leipzig in 1932, interrupted Schmitt’s plea by calling out “situational jurisprudence.” See Preußen contra Reich vor dem Staatsgerichtshof. Stenogrammbericht der Verhandlungen vor dem Staatsgerichtshof in Leipzig vom 10. bis 14. und vom 17. Oktober 1932, Berlin 1933, p. 464.

“CDU deputy Nellen” — On 3 July 1956, Bundestag deputy Peter Nellen raised objections to provisions governing conscientious objection in the Conscription Act, arguing that in his view they restricted a fundamental right. See Der Spiegel, 1956, no. 29, pp. 9–11. After repeated disagreements with his party, Nellen moved to the SPD in 1959.

“Letter from Rabbi Jacob Taubes” — To Armin Mohler, 14 February 1952. The religious philosopher Jacob Taubes (1923–1987), a friend of Mohler, was at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem from 1951 to 1953. The letter, in which Taubes describes his tense and complicated relationship with Carl Schmitt, is printed in BW Taubes, pp. 130–37. Schmitt received the letter from Mohler and circulated copies among acquaintances; see BW Mohler, pp. 116, 119.
“Hans Zehrer: All disaster comes from the Renaissance” — See Hans Zehrer, Der Mensch in dieser Welt, Hamburg 1948.

“Bacon of Verulam’s buccinatores” — Schmitt quotes from the following edition: Francis Bacon, Fr. Baconi De Verulamio Sermones fideles …, Lugduni Batavorum 1644; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 23412. The passage is not on p. 248, however, but on pp. 241–42:

Attamen, sine controversia, hujusmodi ingeniis, in Civilibus, aliquando uti prodest. Si fama excitanda sit, vel opinio late spargenda, sive virtutis, sive potentiae, istiusmodi homines Buccinatores egregii sunt.

“There is, without question, sometimes a certain use for people of this kind in public affairs. When a reputation must be stirred up, or an opinion about someone’s virtue or power spread far and wide, such people make excellent trumpeters.”

“Machiavelli, thou art an Ass” (1640) — A quotation from The Distracted State by the Elizabethan author John Tatham, though the work dates not from 1640 but from 1641. The line is regarded as an early example of people mocking Machiavelli. See John Tatham, The Dramatic Works of John Tatham, New York 1967, p. 46.

“Dio Chrysostom: Christ died as a Haman” — This apparently refers not to Dio Chrysostom but to John Chrysostom and his anti-Jewish work Adversus Judaeos, written around 390. The Codex Theodosianus XVI, 8.18, in 408 prohibited Jews from mocking Christianity by burning an image of Haman on a cross during the festival of Purim. In the Book of Esther, Haman is the highest official at the Persian court and seeks to exterminate the Jews of the Persian Empire.
Sacaea — Festival in honor of the Babylonian goddess Saco.
“white mouse” — Colloquial expression for a police officer.

“Letter from Dr. Kleine” — The lawyer Dr. Heinz Kleine was one of five editors of the Juristenzeitung. In its issue of 9 May 1952, under the heading “Constitutional Law,” pp. 269–72, the journal discussed the danger posed to legislative authority by an expansion of the Federal Constitutional Court’s power of judicial review. The Court is described there as the “guardian of the constitution,” without any mention of Carl Schmitt.
fame futura famelicus — See above, note to p. 179.
Fiat Justitia Pereat Mundus — “Let justice be done, even if the world perishes.” Motto of Emperor Ferdinand I, who reigned from 1556 to 1564.
“Reply to Klug and Klein” — Klein = Kleine; see above, note to p. 275. Klug is probably the jurist Ulrich Klug (1913–1993).
“Konradin, Act 3, Scene 2” — Refers to Konrad Weiß’s drama Konradin von Hohenstaufen.
Deus Venter — quorum deus venter, “whose god is their belly,” Vulgate, Philippians 3:19.

“Bibliography by Mr. Piet Tommissen” — Piet Tommissen (1925–2011), Belgian economist and sociologist, produced the first Carl Schmitt bibliography: Piet Tommissen, Versuch einer Carl-Schmitt-Bibliographie, Düsseldorf 1953; compiled in 1952, with a typescript in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 20492. It later appeared in expanded form in Festschrift für Carl Schmitt zum 70. Geburtstag dargebracht von Freunden und Schülern, ed. Hans Barion, Ernst Forsthoff, Werner Weber, 2nd unchanged ed., Berlin 1989, pp. 273–330.

“If Eduard Spranger confronts me with the questionnaire answer” — See C. Schmitt, “Gespräch mit Eduard Spranger.” In: ECS, pp. 9–12. The question “Are you a Christian?” does not appear there. On the relationship between Schmitt and Spranger, see Schmittiana V, 1996, pp. 205–7; Schmittiana NF II, 2014, pp. 146–52.

“Whoever says God means to deceive” (Proudhon) — Schmitt may be referring to Proudhon’s statement Dieu c’est le mal — “God is evil” — which Schmitt usually renders in the form “Whoever says humanity means to deceive.” See BdP, p. 55.

“Magnificent, what Günther Krauss says” — Günther Krauss, Homo homini homo. Zwölf Kapitel zur Relectio de Indis des Francisco de Vitoria, typescript habilitation thesis, n.d.; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 27110. Krauss’s attempt to qualify as a professor at the University of Bonn with this work failed; van Laak, p. 248, note 46. Schmitt wrote to Forsthoff in 1956 “that Krauss was bound to fail because of his own stubbornness.” BW Forsthoff, p. 127.

“the zeal of Karl Thieme and Romano Guardini for persecution and compensation” — K. Thieme (1902–1963), historian and theologian. For the criticism of Schmitt by Thieme, a friend of Waldemar Gurian, see K. Thieme, “Carl Schmitts Apologie.” In: Deutsche Universitätszeitung, 17 November 1950, p. 18; see also BW Mohler, p. 123; van Laak, pp. 147–48.

R. Guardini (1885–1968), Catholic theologian, held the chair in Philosophy of Religion and Christian Worldview at the University of Berlin from 1923 until his forced retirement in 1939. Schmitt met him in Sombart’s house in 1930; see Tb. 1930–34.
“the grand seigneur of Pasel” — Peterheinrich Kirchhoff; see above, note to p. 75.
Jup — Josef Schmitt (1893–1970), physician and Carl Schmitt’s brother.

Würmeling — Franz-Josef Würmeling (1900–1986), conservative politician and influential member of the CDU. In 1952 he introduced a bill in the Bundestag proposing the adoption of a first-past-the-post electoral system.
“Jehovah, I mock you forever …” — Freely adapted from Heinrich Heine’s poem “Belsazar”:
Jehovah! I mock you forevermore — I am the King of Babylon!
“Nasses Brot, p. 137” — Richard Hasemann, Nasses Brot, Pfullingen 1952, an account of Russian captivity as a prisoner of war.
Pepysm — After Samuel Pepys; see above, note to p. 72.
“A Caliban who knows Greek …” — Schmitt is speaking about Gerhard Nebel; see above, note to p. 269.

“the old Marius’s seventh consulship” — Gaius Marius, c. 156–86 BC, died shortly after beginning his seventh consulship, which he assumed after returning from exile in Africa and taking revenge on his enemies.

“There are noble souls who, in another age, would have said that a king should be put on trial not for the crimes committed during his rule but simply for the crime of having been king. For nothing in the world can legitimize this usurpation. Whatever illusions and conventions monarchy may wrap itself in, it is an eternal crime, against which every human being has the right to rise up and take arms.

“It is one of those outrages that not even the blindness of an entire people can justify. Such a people is guilty before nature because of the example it has set, and from nature all human beings receive the secret mission to exterminate domination in every country.”
Antoine L. de Saint-Just, Opinion concernant le jugement de Louis XVI. Séance du 13 novembre 1792, l’an premier de la République française. In: idem, Oeuvres de Saint-Just, Paris 1834, p. 7.

A. Koestler, Darkness at Noon — Schmitt read the book in French translation: Arthur Koestler, Le zéro et l’infini, Paris 1945. The first German translation appeared in 1946 under the title Sonnenfinsternis.
Rubashov — Nikolai Rubashov is the main character in Koestler’s Darkness at Noon. Schmitt is not quoting literally here, but only paraphrasing.
ecclesia non militans sed intrigans — “a Church that does not fight, but intrigues.”
“He was a man who noticed such things” — Correctly: “He was a man who used to notice such things.” Thomas Hardy, “Afterwards.” In: idem, The Collected Poems of Thomas Hardy, Ware 2002, p. 521.

“see Michel Mourre, Lam[ennais], p. 184” — Michel Mourre, Lamennais ou l’hérésie des temps modernes, Paris 1955. Since the book was not published until 1955, the remark must have been added later. This is also suggested by the fact that it appears on the verso in different ink. Schmitt did not meet the French historian Mourre (1928–1977) until 1954, through Mohler, who also sent him Mourre’s 1955 book on Lamennais. See the index to BW Mohler.
“see Der Spiegel, 38/52” — The issue contains an article about Frank Lloyd Wright under the title “Der amerikanische Ausdruck.”
